metadata.summary: Background: The molecular mechanisms underlying heart failure (HF) following myocardial infarction (MI) (HF-MI) remain incompletely understood, and whole-transcriptome profiling studies hold significant promise for disease prevention and treatment. Methods: Whole-transcriptome sequencing was performed on post-MI patients with and without HF to analyze differentially expressed mRNAs, lncRNAs, and circRNAs, along with functional enrichment analysis. Co-expression networks linking lncRNA-mRNA and circRNA-mRNA pairs, as well as ceRNA networks involving lncRNA-miRNA-mRNA and circRNA-miRNA-mRNA interactions, were constructed for differentially expressed (DE) RNAs. Key lncRNAs were validated by RT-qPCR. Transcriptional factor-lncRNA networks were constructed, and key relationships were verified using RIP-PCR. Results: Patients with HF-MI exhibited marked elevation of NT-proBNP and significant reduction in LVEF%. Transcriptome-wide analysis revealed 228 DE-mRNAs, 700 DE-lncRNAs, and 1188 DE-circRNAs in HF-MI compared to non-heart failure patients (NHF-MI). Construction of the ceRNA network identified hsa-miR-6089 and hsa-miR-6771-5p as key miRNAs in the lncRNA-miRNA-mRNA network, while hsa-miR-1207-5p and hsa-miR-10392-3p were key miRNAs in the circRNA-miRNA-mRNA network. PVT1, SNHG5, TTN-AS1, HCP5, and OIP5-AS1 were identified as the five key DE-lncRNAs, with PVT1/SNHG5 showing upregulation and TTN-AS1/HCP5/OIP5-AS1 exhibiting downregulation. The transcription factor-lncRNA network primarily involves GLIS3-HCP5 and ZNF135-PVT1, with validated associative interactions. Conclusion: This study systematically mapped the regulatory network of HF-MI, revealing the roles of the GLIS3-HCP5 and ZNF135-PVT1 regulatory axes in HF-MI, thereby providing a basis for exploring novel therapeutic strategies.

Background.Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2D) involves progressive pancreatic beta-cell dysfunction, but conserved islet programs require cross-cohort and single-cell validation.

Methods.We integrated four human islet transcriptomic cohorts using differential expression, random-effects meta-analysis, Hallmark scoring, and module scoring. To test generalizability without reusing held-out outcomes, modules were re-derived from three cohorts and scored in the fourth in rotating study-level cross-fitting, with expression-and detection-matched random gene-set nulls. Machine-learning performance in GSE164416 was estimated by nested stratified 5-fold cross-validation with DEG calling and feature selection repeated within each outer training fold. An annotation-compatible score was tested in GSE50244, and beta-cell validation used GSE221156.

Results.Cross-fitted IsletDysfunctionScore effects were positive in all four held-out cohorts (d = 0.39-1.36; pooled Hedges g = 0.905, 95% CI 0.501-1.309, p = 1.14 x 10^-5, I2 = 5.5%). Matched gene-set null testing supported effects beyond random expectation in two cohorts. Nested machine learning yielded AUC = 0.960 (bootstrap 95% CI 0.900-0.997); GABRA2 and ENSG00000284653 were selected in all outer folds. The external 8-gene consensus-pool score achieved AUC = 0.907 (DeLong 95% CI 0.818-0.996), but its fixed threshold did not transfer. In GSE221156, the single-cell dysfunction-score analog increased and BetaIdentitySecretion decreased in T2D; ImmuneStress was nominally increased but did not survive false-discovery correction across the single-cell score family.

Conclusions.Human T2D islets show a reproducible stress/identity-loss framework that generalizes directionally under study-level cross-fitting and beta-cell-resolved validation. The candidate panel is a research transcriptomic signature requiring further validation.
observations.title: Human Islet Transcriptomics in Type 2 Diabetes Reveals Conserved Dysfunction Axes and a Candidate Gene Panel

observations.text: High attrition rates across clinical drug development impose immense clinical and financial burdens, yet prospectively forecasting whether an individual trial will achieve its primary endpoint remains challenging. Here we present a machine-learning system that predicts clinical trial success across phases I-IV, independently modeling studies with efficacy versus safety/toxicity primary endpoints. To prevent lookahead bias and outcome leakage, models are trained on registration-time features, including target and mechanism-of-action precedent, drug modality and novelty, trial design and operational characteristics, and frozen literature-derived target-choice embeddings. Each prediction yields a continuous Predictive Trial Index (PTI) between 0 and 1 reflecting success probability. On a test set of trials initiated in 2021 or later, the efficacy model achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.828 (95% CI 0.812-0.845; n = 2,347) and the safety/toxicity model reached 0.809 (95% CI 0.787-0.831; n = 1,485). These models are embedded in inClinico Agent, an agentic AI system integrating frontier large language models (LLMs) with deterministic scoring engines, retrieval tools and specialized clinical skills. We also introduce ClinicoBench, a prospective benchmark of 3,235 ongoing trials evaluated by inClinico Agent and five frontier LLMs, establishing a leakage-free foundation for tracking prospective predictive accuracy as trials reach completion.
observations.title: inClinico Agent for clinical trial endpoint prediction and prospective evaluation

metadata.summary: Background: Acute myocardial infarction (AMI) followed by a reperfusion results in a phasic response by cardiac macrophages. During the first 7 days after AMI, macrophage populations exhibit dynamic phenotypic changes. Ultimately, inflammatory damage results in ventricular remodeling and fibrosis. Macrophages are critical to cardiac function and long-term prognoses. Objective: Elucidate the spatiotemporal behavior of specific macrophage subtypes during  AMI and identify novel genes with prospective therapeutic potential. Methods: We implement an IRI mouse model of AMI to assess cardiac macrophage behavior during AMI. RCM were isolated using flow cytometry and analyzed with NanoString. Pathway enrichment analysis annotated statistically significant genes. We employed transcriptome-wide, spatiotemporal analysis of cardiac tissue samples during  AMI.

observations.title: Transcriptomic characterization of macrophage subtype and behavior in early stage myocardial infarction

metadata.summary: Myocardial infarction (MI) causes cardiomyocyte loss and fibrotic scar formation, disrupting electrical communication and impairing cardiac function. Conductive hydrogels have been studied to reconstruct an electroactive microenvironment for the infarcted myocardium, yet their regenerative effect is limited by the impaired function of surviving cardiomyocytes. Here, we developed a mechanoelectrically active and paintable hydrogel capable of converting cardiac motion into localized electrical stimulation to repair infarcted myocardium. The paintable nature of the hydrogel enables easy application onto irregular epicardial surfaces using a customized brush, while subsequent photocrosslinking allows selective adhesion of the hydrogel to only epicardial surfaces, not to surrounding tissues. Under cyclic loading and in contracting cardiac organoids, the hydrogel generated physiologically relevant electrical potentials, demonstrating efficient deformation-induced charge generation. In a rat MI model, the hydrogel providing electrostimulation alleviated ventricular wall thinning and fibrosis, promoted neovascularization and M2 macrophage polarization, and improved cardiac function. Transcriptomic analysis further revealed upregulation of genes involved in myocardial contraction and energy metabolism. As such, our study offers a minimally invasive and clinically translatable approach for cardiac repair and other tissue applications.

observations.title: Paintable Mechanoelectric Hydrogel Integrating Conductivity and Piezoelectricity for Myocardial Infarction Repair

observations.text: Verticality perception is the sense of ones body orientation relative to gravity. It can be disrupted by neurological diseases or during aviation and space flight, resulting in falls and accidents. This perception is thought to arise from integration of vestibular and visual signals, yet where this multisensory computation is spatially implemented in the human brain remains unresolved. Room tilt illusion (RTI), in which the visual environment abruptly reorients relative to gravity (typically by 90{degrees} or 180{degrees}), has been proposed as a model disorder for studying verticality perception. Here, we leverage focal brain lesions (predominantly ischemic or hemorrhagic strokes) causing RTI to localize this multisensory computation. We assembled a total of 37 patients with brain lesions causing RTI from a systematic literature search and local cases across two centers. Clinical data were tabulated and lesions were analyzed using multimodal voxel- and connectome-based lesion mapping methods. Lesion findings were further tested against an independent dataset of 509 direct electrical stimulation sites associated with vestibular or non-vestibular percepts. The RTI lesions were distributed across cortical and subcortical locations, with the cerebellum representing the most frequent lesion site (49%). Despite anatomical heterogeneity, lesion connectivity converged on two hub regions: one in the posterior cerebellum and another in the mid-cingulate cortex. This pattern was robust to methodological variations, separation of RTI subtypes, and exclusion of cerebellar lesions. This pattern was also specific to RTI when compared against 185 phenotypically matched lesions from patients with milder disturbances of verticality perception and 1,110 lesions associated with 27 other neuropsychiatric syndromes. Finally, independent direct electrical stimulation data converged on both lesion-derived RTI hubs (mid-cingulate cortex: g=0.62, p<.001; posterior cerebellum: g=0.34, p=.014, 10,000 label permutations). In conclusion, anatomically diverse RTI lesions localize to a specific cerebello-cingulate network, providing an anatomical framework for verticality perception in the human brain. Our findings generate testable hypotheses for experimentally modulating or protecting verticality perception in neurological patients or pilots.
observations.title: Lesions causing room tilt illusion link a cerebello-cingulate brain network to verticality perception

metadata.summary: This study generated a transcriptome-wide resource of peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) from two clinical groups: subjects with hyperuricemia (HUA, n=15) and subjects with coronary artery disease together with hyperuricemia (CHD_HUA, n=15). Total RNA was extracted from PBMC and poly(A)+ mRNA was enriched with oligo(dT) magnetic beads. Strand-specific libraries were constructed using dUTP incorporation and UDG second-strand digestion, and paired-end 150 bp sequencing was performed on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000. Clean reads were aligned to the Homo sapiens reference genome with HISAT2, and transcripts were assembled and quantified with StringTie. Gene-level raw read counts and FPKM values for all 30 samples are provided as processed data, together with the paired-end FASTQ files. The dataset is intended to support investigation of transcriptional differences between hyperuricemia and coronary artery disease with hyperuricemia.

metadata.summary: Obesity-induced metabolic cardiomyopathy features myocardial lipid overload, mitochondrial dysfunction and chronic inflammation, with few targeted therapies. Hyodeoxycholic acid (HDCA), a natural secondary bile acid, plays key roles in metabolic homeostasis, yet its direct cardioprotective effects in obesity-related cardiac injury remain unclear. Here, we investigated HDCA effects on high-fat diet-induced cardiomyopathy using in vivo, lipotoxic cardiomyocyte and 3D cardiac spheroid models. HDCA ameliorated cardiac dysfunction, hypertrophic remodeling and myocardial lipid accumulation. Transcriptomics showed HDCA remodelled cardiac programs governing mitochondrial and lipid metabolism as well as inflammation. Mechanistically, HDCA limited cardiomyocyte lipid uptake via TGR5-dependent suppression of CD36 membrane localization, boosted mitochondrial respiration and ATP production, and reduced oxidative stress. HDCA also bound PIK3CA to inhibit PI3K-AKT-mediated inflammation. In 3D cardiac spheroids, HDCA alleviated lipotoxic injury. Collectively, HDCA protects against obesity-associated cardiomyopathy by coordinating myocardial lipid metabolism, mitochondrial homeostasis and inflammatory signaling, representing a promising candidate for metabolic heart disease.

observations.title: Hyodeoxycholic acid protects against obesity-associated cardiomyopathy by restoring myocardial metabolic homeostasis and suppressing inflammatory remodeling

metadata.summary: Laminopathies comprise a diverse array of phenotypes that involve multiple organs and are caused by mutations in the LMNA gene, which encodes nuclear envelope protein lamin A (LMNA). Cardiac involvement is a prominent feature and a major cause of mortality and morbidity in laminopathies. LMNA interacts with chromatin through lamin-associated domains (LADs) and regulates gene expression. The role of the LMNA in regulating chromatin structure and gene expression in cardiac myocytes is unknown.  We conditionally deleted the Lmna gene specifically in cardiac myocytes in the mouse, isolated the LMNA-deficient cardiac myocytes, and characterized genomic structure and function at two levels: first, by identifying and characterizing the genome-wide CTCF binding sites by a CUT&RUN assay; and second, the chromatin conformational changes by HiC.  To determine the role of LMNA in genome organization and gene expression we integrated CTCF binding, LAD, Hi-C data with the gene expression (RNA-seq), and DNA double-stranded breaks (DSBs), determined by END-Seq, in cardiac myocytes.  Compared to wild-type (WT) myocytes, LMNA deficiency increased genomic occupancy of CTCF , predominantly outside of the constitutive LADs (cLADs), and increased gene expression at the CTCF binding sites. Likewise, DSBs were highly enriched at the CTCF binding sites. However, only a small fraction of the chromatin compartments was shifted in the LMNA-deficient cardiac myocytes. LMNA-deficiency changed the organization of one-third of the topologically-associated domains (TADs). The changes were characterized by the merger of 2 or more TADs (60%), mainly in the non-LAD regions, splitting (30%), and shifting boundaries (10%). Reorganization of TADs, however, did not directly affect gene expression or the prevalence of DSBs. A remarkable effect of the LMNA deficiency was on chromatin loops, as it led to a gain of ~ 600 and a loss of ~1000 loops, whose boundaries were enriched in the CTCF binding sites. The changes affected the transcript level of ~25% of the differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in the LMNA-deficient cardiac myocytes. The gain of the loop was associated with increased gene expression, whereas the loss of the loop had the opposite effect. A multivariate analysis showed that differential CTCF  binding  (largest), loops, and cLADs affected the transcript levels of the DEGs, whereas TADs and chromatin compartments appeared to act in concert with these factors  rather than as independent determinants.  In conclusion, LMNA regulates chromatin structure like TADs its role in  gene expression is mediated mainly through CTCF, cLADs, and loops,. The findings provide insights into the molecular pathogenesis of cardiac involvement in the diverse array of phenotypes in laminopathies.

observations.title: Effects of the Lamin A on Chromatin Structure and Function in Cardiac Myocytes in a Mouse Model of Lamin-Cardiomyopathy

metadata.summary: Truncating variants in desmoplakin (DSP) are a leading cause of arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, a severe heart muscle disease characterized by fibrosis and life-threatening arrhythmias. Desmoplakin anchors the junctions that hold heart muscle cells together to the internal cytoskeleton, enabling the heart to withstand the force of each contraction. No targeted therapy exists, and DSP is too large for conventional gene replacement. Here we show, in explanted human hearts and in human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes, that truncating DSP variants reduce desmoplakin RNA and protein, and that the resulting haploinsufficiency renders cardiomyocytes vulnerable to cell–cell adhesion failure under contractile stress, preceded by disruption of the cell membrane. Lowering contractile force with the myosin inhibitor mavacamten prevents this failure. Circumventing the size of DSP, CRISPR-based transcriptional activation of the endogenous gene restores desmoplakin expression and rescues adhesion. Haploinsufficiency is therefore the primary defect in DSP cardiomyopathy, and transcriptional activation offers a therapeutic strategy.

observations.title: Desmoplakin Haploinsufficiency Underlies Cell-Cell Adhesion Failure in DSP Cardiomyopathy and is Rescued by Transcriptional Activation

metadata.summary: Diabetic cardiomyopathy is a clinical condition of ventricular dysfunction, with obesity and insulin resistance as the primary risk factors. Under this condition, the heart accumulates fatty acids and encounters lipotoxicity, which impairs cardiac insulin sensitivity and leads to cardiomyopathy. Angiotensin-(1-9) is a peptide of the counter-regulatory axis of the renin-angiotensin system with cardioprotective effects in myocardial infarction. However, its role in diabetic cardiomyopathy is unknown. To explore the role of angiotensin-(1-9), we first induced lipotoxic stress in the heart by high-fat diet (HFD) feeding in mice. Angiotensin-(1-9) was then administered for four weeks using osmotic mini-pumps. Cardiac function was assessed by, and insulin sensitivity was evaluated in tissues after a bolus of insulin injection. Moreover, lipotoxic stress in vitro was modeled by high glucose medium plus palmitate in neonatal rat ventricular myocytes (NRVMs). We show that angiotensin-(1-9) improves myocardial function and reverts pathological cardiac remodeling in mice. Moreover, angiotensin-(1-9) enhances whole-body glucose tolerance and reduces homeostatic model assessment of insulin resistance (HOMA-IR). We next demonstrate that angiotensin-(1-9) increases insulin sensitivity in the heart and skeletal muscle but not in adipose tissue or the liver. Mechanistically, angiotensin-(1-9) does not affect insulin signaling in cardiomyocytes at baseline, while it significantly improves insulin action under lipotoxic stress through AT2 receptor (AT2R) and PKA. These findings demonstrate that angiotensin-(1-9) improves cardiac function under metabolic challenge and promotes insulin signaling in cardiomyocytes under lipotoxicity, which may shed light on the therapeutic exploration against diabetic cardiomyopathy.

observations.title: Angiotensin-(1-9) protects cardiomyocytes under lipotoxic stress by AT2 receptor

To further investigate the function of IRAG1 in vascular smooth muscle cells, we performed siRNA-mediated knockdown of IRAG1 in human coronary artery smooth muscle cells (HCASMCs), followed by bulk RNA-seq 48 hours after transfection. Differential gene analysis revealed that IRAG1 knockdown induced transcriptional programs associated with proliferation and inflammatory responses.

metadata.summary: Background: Reactive oxygen species are increased across most pulmonary hypertension (PH) etiologies, resulting in increased reactive lipid dicarbonyls, which form protein adducts and impair mitochondrial function. We hypothesized that reducing reactive lipids would reduce right ventricular systolic pressure (RVSP) and improve cardiac function by eliminating protein-lipid damage feedback loops. Methods: We used 2-hydroxybenzylamine (2-HOBA) to scavenge reactive lipids in three complimentary mouse models of PH: AKR-high fat diet (HFD, metabolic stress), LNAME-HFD (cardiometabolic syndrome), and pulmonary artery banding (PAB, load stress). Cardiac function was measured by echocardiography and catheterization. RV energy metabolism was determined by oxygraphy. Mass spectrometry analyzed lipids and ceramides; O-link and RNA-Seq evaluated proteomic and gene expression in lungs, RV, and LV. Results: Reducing reactive lipids with 2-HOBA resulted in a ~10% reduction in RVSP, reduced diastolic dysfunction, reduced plasma lipids and ceramides, and normalized RV fatty acid oxidation that was severely impaired in the AKR-HFD and PAB models. Proteomic and RNA changes in the lungs, RV, and LV suggested reduced oxidative damage and inflammatory signaling and altered developmental and actin organization signaling; these changes are plausibly associated with the improved adaptation. Some changes were sex specific, including a 4x higher cardiac fatty acid content in males than females. Conclusions: Reactive lipid scavenging improves cardiac metabolic and diastolic function and pulmonary vascular resistance through restoration of mitochondrial function and reduced oxidative protein damage. The magnitude of hemodynamic improvement combined with substantial diastolic function improvement suggests clinical potential, particularly for PH patients with metabolic comorbidities.

metadata.summary: Background. Rheumatic heart valve disease (RHVD) is the leading cause of acquired valvular disease worldwide, driven by autoimmune responses that sustain chronic inflammation and fibrotic remodeling, predominantly affecting the mitral valve (MV). Although immune dysregulation and transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) signaling are implicated, the molecular mechanisms underlying disease progression and their relationship to clinical severity remain incompletely defined. Methods. We performed a tissue-centric multi-omics study combining histopathology, unbiased proteomics of human MV tissue (n=72), and plasma proteomics from an external cohort (n=445). We associated proteomic signatures with clinical parameters. Cross-species validation involved single-cell RNA sequencing from a murine model of autoimmune valvular carditis. Mechanistic studies used primary human valvular interstitial cells (VICs) and a three-dimensional MV mimetics. Results. RHVD MVs exhibited leaflet thickening, fibrosis, immune cell infiltration, and neovascularization, with T-cell abundance correlating with tissue remodeling. Proteomic profiling identified 1,436 differentially expressed proteins enriched in extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling, immune response, hemostasis, and multi-growth factor signaling, including TGF-β and insulin-like growth factor binding protein (IGFBP) pathway. Integrated tissue-plasma analysis revealed shared molecular signatures. The mean transvalvular gradient captured the hemodynamic continuum from mitral regurgitation to stenosis and was associated with coordinated with ECM remodeling, cytoskeletal, immune, and hemostatic pathways. Cross-species integration confirmed convergence on ECM remodeling, immune activation, and TGF-β/IGFBP signaling, predominantly in VIC and myofibroblast populations. Mechanistically, TGF-β induced IGFBP5, IGFBP7, and CCN2 expression in VICs, while their silencing attenuated collagen expression. MV mimetics exposed to pro-fibrotic and inflammatory stimuli recapitulated these findings. Conclusions. TGF-β-centered signaling networks drive the coordinated immune, and fibrotic remodeling that characterizes RHVD. The TGF-β-IGFBP axis emerges as a key mediator of VIC-driven fibrosis and links molecular remodeling to clinical disease progression, highlighting novel therapeutic opportunities.

metadata.summary: Reperfusion of ischemic myocardium triggers a sterile inflammatory cascade in which NF-κB–dependent transcriptional priming precedes NLRP3 inflammasome assembly and caspase-1 activation. Diacerein, approved for osteoarthritis, is converted in vivo to rhein, an NF-κB inhibitor with inflammasome-attenuating properties, but its effect on the ischemic myocardial transcriptome is unknown.  To define the transcriptional program underlying diacerein-mediated cardioprotection, male Wistar rats received oral diacerein (80 mg/kg/day) or vehicle for 10 days before the heart was isolated and subjected to global no-flow ischemia followed by reperfusion in a Langendorff preparation. RNA sequencing of left ventricular tissue identified 314 differentially expressed genes (268 downregulated, 46 upregulated) in diacerein- versus vehicle-treated hearts. Downregulated genes included Selp (P-selectin), the endothelial adhesion molecule mediating leukocyte capture, Csf2rb (the shared GM-CSF/IL-3/IL-5 receptor subunit), and Ripk1, while Card9 was upregulated. Gene set enrichment analysis showed suppression of TNF signaling, NF-κB signaling, and cytokine–cytokine receptor interaction pathways.  These data indicate that diacerein pretreatment suppresses leukocyte recruitment and inflammatory priming programs in the ischemic myocardium, and provide a transcriptional basis for its cardioprotective effect.

observations.text:
Summary / Abstract

BackgroundModels based on administrative population health records can help improve understanding of disease and hospitalisation risk. This understanding can support evidence-based population health policy and processes. Influenza and other acute respiratory diseases place a large, inequitable burden on the New Zealand population and health care resources. We have developed and evaluated such models using retrospective New Zealand hospitalisation records linked to other administrative data to estimate individual-level risk of hospitalisation due to acute respiratory infection.

MethodsWe analysed linked annual records for approximately 4{middle dot}85-5{middle dot}36 million people in 2017-2024. Six machine learning algorithms and eight variable sets were assessed using five-fold cross-validation grouped by demographic profile. Variables comprised demographics, continuous hospital-based (M3) and pharmaceutical-based (P3) morbidity indices, and influenza vaccination status. Models trained on one year were also evaluated on data from the following year. Performance measures were the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and the average precision score (APS). SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) described model contributions, including paired vaccination-input changes in 2024.

FindingsAnnual national hospitalisation prevalence ranged from 1{middle dot}01% to 1{middle dot}60%. With all variables, mean cross-validation AUROC and APS were 0{middle dot}8430 and 0{middle dot}1283 for LightGBM (LGB), and 0{middle dot}8415 and 0{middle dot}1285 for XGBoost (XGB). Adding both morbidity indices to the demographics increased LGB APS from 0{middle dot}0720 to 0{middle dot}1158; adding vaccination further increased it to 0{middle dot}1283. Next-year AUROC and APS averaged 0{middle dot}8429 and 0{middle dot}1267 for LGB and 0{middle dot}8423 and 0{middle dot}1277 for XGB. Age and morbidity were the most influential variables. Among vaccinated individuals, SHAP analysis indicated that vaccination contributed most strongly towards lower model-estimated hospitalisation risk in the oldest age group.

InterpretationCombining historical morbidity and vaccination information in gradient boosting models improved the ability to distinguish between people who experienced respiratory hospitalisation and those who did not in annual New Zealand population data. Similar next-year performance and interpretable variation across age and morbidity profiles support further development toward practical risk assessment, including calibration and evaluation across population groups.

Research in contextO_ST_ABSEvidence before this studyC_ST_ABSOur focused narrative review considered population-based respiratory hospitalisation models, respiratory disease burden in New Zealand, and the development of the M3 and P3 morbidity indices. Existing studies include population models for COVID-19 and infant respiratory syncytial virus, risk-factor analyses of broad respiratory admissions, and evidence that hospital and pharmaceutical morbidity measures provide complementary information.

Added value of this studyThis is the first evaluation of national hospitalisation data linked to other national administrative data to model the risk of acute respiratory infection admission across eight annual datasets, comparing six algorithms and eight variable sets. Together with the benchmark results, these findings illustrate how gradient boosting applied to population-scale records can represent and explain combinations of routinely recorded health information.

Implications of all the available evidenceQuantifying historical morbidity and including vaccination information improved respiratory hospitalisation classification, with gradient boosting providing the strongest overall performance. The explanatory analyses further showed that vaccination-related contributions depended on the individuals age and morbidity profile. Representing these clinically plausible patterns supports the use of flexible, non-linear models, such as tree-based algorithms, and rich population-scale records for developing interpretable respiratory risk assessments. The study establishes a basis for a New Zealand respiratory risk model by identifying effective algorithms and useful combinations of variables.
observations.title: Population-scale machine learning models to estimate individual-level risk for acute respiratory infection

metadata.summary: Nuclear receptor subfamily 4 group A member 2 (NR4A2) is a widely expressed immediate early gene induced by a host of physiological signals such as growth factors, cytokines, and neurotransmitters. In the adult mammalian heart, including in cardiomyocytes, NR4A2 mRNAs increase more than 60-fold in response to beta-adrenergic stimulation. However, the nature of the transcriptional remodeling induced by NR4A2 in the stressed heart has remained poorly investigated. We show here that NR4A2 activation in mouse cardiomyocytes leads to a rapid remodeling of the cardiac microRNA network. A total of 35 miRNAs were down-regulated, including the muscle-specific miR-133a and miR-499. On the opposite, 65 miRNAs were up-regulated, with a strong representation of miRNAs encoded within the imprinted Dlk1-Dio3 domain. Non-coding RNAs from the Dlk1-Dio3 locus are known for coordinating critical steps of cardiac development such as cardiac lineage commitment, cardiac morphogenesis, and cardiomyocyte proliferation, and for inhibiting mitochondrial function in myocytes. The findings shed light on a novel regulatory mechanism controlling cardiac homeostasis, and establish a framework to investigate further the roles played by NR4A2 in cardiac adaptation or maladaptation to various acute and pathological stress conditions.

metadata.summary: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is an X-linked fatal disorder caused by dystrophin deficiency, characterized by early-onset, progressive degeneration of skeletal and cardiac muscle. Although microdystrophin (µDys) gene therapies provide functional benefit and partially restore tissue architecture, their impact on disease-associated cellular programs remains unclear. We evaluated proprietary codon-optimized µDys delivered via AAV8 under the MHCK7 promoter and a MyoD enhancer in severe DMD rats with an exon 52 deletion (DMDdel52). Therapy achieved sustained µDys expression with 90-97% of myofibers and cardiomyocytes, with proteins levels ranging from physiological to supra-physiological. Treatment preserved muscle function and extended survival beyond the median lifespan of untreated DMDdel52 rats, maintaining ambulation, climbing, weight gain, and muscle strength. Treatment also preserved cardiac architecture and function while preventing myonecrosis and adverse remodeling, with no detectable toxicity despite high µDys expression. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing revealed that µDys treatment prevented disease-associated inflammatory and fibrotic activation of fibro-adipogenic progenitors, preserved a pro-regenerative interstitial environment and muscle stem cell quiescence while preventing senescence marker expression. These findings indicate that early µDys gene therapy preserves muscle homeostasis, function, and lifespan by preventing disease-associated cellular programs from becoming established within the regenerative niche of DMD rats.

observations.title: Optimized microdystrophin gene therapy preserves muscle homeostasis and extends survival in DMDdel52 rats

metadata.summary: Truncating variants in desmoplakin (DSP) are a leading cause of arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, a severe heart muscle disease characterized by fibrosis and life-threatening arrhythmias. Desmoplakin anchors the junctions that hold heart muscle cells together to the internal cytoskeleton, enabling the heart to withstand the force of each contraction. No targeted therapy exists, and DSP is too large for conventional gene replacement. Here we show, in explanted human hearts and in human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes, that truncating DSP variants reduce desmoplakin RNA and protein, and that the resulting haploinsufficiency renders cardiomyocytes vulnerable to cell–cell adhesion failure under contractile stress, preceded by disruption of the cell membrane. Lowering contractile force with the myosin inhibitor mavacamten prevents this failure. Circumventing the size of DSP, CRISPR-based transcriptional activation of the endogenous gene restores desmoplakin expression and rescues adhesion. Haploinsufficiency is therefore the primary defect in DSP cardiomyopathy, and transcriptional activation offers a therapeutic strategy.

observations.text: CYP1A2 contributes 13-15% of hepatic CYP450 content and plays a critical role in the metabolism of approximately 10% of pharmaceutical drugs in the human body. CYP1A2 has been previously reported to bioactivate and detoxify both the thion (P=S) and oxon (P=O) forms of organophosphorus (OP) compounds. In this study, we determined the capacity of CYP1A2 to degrade OP compounds using LC-MS/MS, as well as the inhibition of its activity by OP compounds using the previously developed pFluor50 assay. CYP1A2 was selective in metabolizing thions over oxons, and several OP compounds inhibited its activity in a time- and dose-dependent manner. To further investigate the mechanism of CYP1A2-OP interactions, molecular docking studies were performed using a crystal structure of CYP1A2 (PDB ID: 2HI4). Linear correlation analysis between CYP1A2 inhibition at 10 M with 30 minute preincubation and the % OP compound remaining at 2 hours (R = -0.71, P<0.001) showed a moderate but significant correlation. Based on these findings, CYP1A2 was identified as a potential bioscavenger for OP compound metabolism, supporting the future integration of experimental and in silico data for developing artificial intelligence (AI) / machine learning (ML) models for prediction of CYP1A2-mediated metabolism of existing and emerging OP compounds, including those of toxicological and chemical warfare relevance.

observations.text: Cutaneous T cell lymphoma (CTCL) comprises a clinically and molecularly heterogeneous group of skin-homing non-Hodgkin lymphomas for which robust biomarkers remain limited. Prior single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) studies have provided important insights into CTCL biology, but many of these prior studies have been limited by small sample sizes and focused on niche questions of interest. Additionally, many studies have suffered from pseudoreplication, resulting in inflated test statistics and reduced external validity. Here, we assembled and integrated scRNA-seq data spanning 244 unique samples and 132 patients across CTCL, healthy control (HC), and benign inflammatory dermatoses (BID) conditions, generating the most diverse atlas of CTCL to date. Following identification of malignant cell populations and heterogeneous, within-sample gene expression alterations, we applied pseudobulk aggregation and robust linear mixed-effects modeling to nominate recurrent changes across this highly heterogeneous patient cohort. Interrogation of the skin microenvironment identified significant compositional and cell type-specific expression changes in CTCL lesions as compared to control lesions and across clinical stages of disease. Finally, we used unbiased clustering to identify stable, molecularly defined subtypes of disease that were predictive of outcome in an independent dataset. Together, this study provides a rigorous analysis of the most diverse scRNA-seq dataset of CTCL ever compiled, nominating specific alterations in cell type composition and gene expression across malignant cell and microenvironmental populations with significant clinical implications.
observations.title: Large-scale integrated single-cell analysis reveals molecular subtypes and microenvironmental remodeling in cutaneous T cell lymphoma

observations.text: Expansion Microscopy (ExM) enables nanoscale imaging of biological samples while preserving structural and molecular details. The Robust Non-rigid Registration Challenge for ExM (RnR-ExM) was launched to benchmark 3D registration algorithms on real-world ExM datasets. The challenge released 24 pairs of high-resolution 3D volumes from zebrafish, mouse, and C.~elegans, deliberately selected for their difficulty with standard alignment methods. To evaluate performance, we provided curated segmentation masks of nuclei and blood vessels as landmarks for half of the dataset. To encourage learning-based approaches, we released code for generating synthetic training data reflecting the deformation and appearance of the unlabeled pairs. By submission, 168 participants registered, with six teams submitting results by the deadline; the top three were invited to present at ISBI 2023. Accurate registration of ExM volumes is essential for downstream biological analyses such as multiplexed molecular mapping and cell-type-specific structural profiling. In this paper, we detail the methods and results of these top teams, highlighting current capabilities and future directions for 3D registration in ExM. All datasets and code are available at https://rnr-exm.grand-challenge.org/

metadata.summary: Muscle LIM Protein (MLP) is a key component of the cardiomyocyte Z disc that is essential for sarcomere integrity and cardiac homeostasis.  Loss of MLP function results in (cardio)myopathy phenotypes in animal models and is associated with inherited cardiomyopathies in humans. Here, we identify MLP as an evolutionarily conserved non-canonical RNA-binding protein and uncover RNA binding as a previously unrecognized mechanism involved in its cytoskeletal association. Using enhanced RNA interactome capture together with complementary biochemical approaches, we demonstrate direct RNA binding by MLP and map two short RNA-binding motifs adjacent to its LIM domains. Disrupting these motifs markedly reduces RNA association, including residues associated with cardiomyopathies. Mechanistically, RNA is required for MLP’s interactions with cytoskeletal proteins, and for the formation of higher-order MLP-containing assemblies. Consistently, RNA-binding-deficient MLP mutants exhibit impaired interactions with cytoskeletal proteins and reduced cytoskeletal retention. Our findings reveal the importance of RNA binding for the formation of MLP assemblies, and support the emerging role of RNA as a co-factor in the organization of macromolecular complexes, with potential relevance to human disease.
